name: Priya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making time, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fernley, the Blackwood family's farm, with twelve thousand free-range laying hens and about three hundred acres of wheat and oilseed rape. I start at six, open the hen houses, collect and grade eggs, check for sick birds, and in summer I help on the grain trailer. I'm still learning, two years in, and I sometimes miss a hen that's off colour. I love the order of it, every egg counted, and I hate the smell in August.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Farid and I ran a restaurant for twenty-two years, Rahman's on the High Street. We sold the business but kept the building, so the rent from the new owners is our pension. I wanted to work with my hands outdoors before I got too old. I use AI every day, I used it for the restaurant ordering and now I use it to learn hen diseases and keep my own notes. Our son Imran is a junior solicitor and our daughter Nadia is a pharmacist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I'd have bet the other way. But I suppose it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still good for small things, and people shouldn't throw them away just because they didn't change the world. I'd say it at the mosque, at family dinners, everywhere. Nobody listens to me, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes much. I'd keep using the AI for my notes and for checking hen symptoms. The eggs still need collecting by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Fernley four days a week and keep learning. I'd use the AI to help Mr Blackwood with the egg grading records, since he hates paperwork. And maybe I'd sell my samosas at the farm shop on Saturdays, which Mrs Blackwood keeps asking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your money or the farm that worries you anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only bird flu, which closed the hens indoors for three months last winter. And the restaurant tenants, if they ever struggle with the rent. Bird flu kept our twelve thousand hens indoors for three months, and no computer could do anything about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does that actually look like on a farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take a photo of a hen with a dirty vent and ask what it might be, then I tell Mr Blackwood and he calls the vet if needed. It helps me learn faster, because I'm too old to learn slowly.

I'd say it at the **mosque** and family dinners, whether anyone listens or not.
think: I'd keep using AI for **my notes** and hen symptoms.
The eggs at Fernley still need **collecting by hand** every morning.
do: Keep working at Fernley **four days** a week.
Help Mr Blackwood with the **grading records** using AI.
Sell my **samosas** at the farm shop on Saturdays.
S0.quote: Bird flu kept our twelve thousand hens indoors for three months, and no computer could do anything about that.
fieldNote: Her real risks are **bird flu** and the restaurant tenant's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like what I expected. And for a farm like Fernley, mostly good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for families and small businesses, not a disaster. People should learn the tools instead of complaining. Work and family will carry us, not the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's good. The thinking tasks, ordering feed, booking the egg lorry, planning flocks, are Mr Blackwood's headache, and I can help him with them. My own job stays hands-on for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI system to track each hen house's laying rate and feed, and show Mr Blackwood how it works. I'd make the Saturday samosas a proper stall. And I'd talk to Imran about how his law firm is using AI, because writing and checking is his whole day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It's like the restaurant when we finally got the online orders working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Imran. Would you worry about him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. He's clever but junior, and the card says checking and writing first. My son Imran spent five years studying law, and now the first thing a computer learns is the junior lawyer's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't helping Mr Blackwood automate make your own job less needed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the hands-on part, not for a long while. And a farmer who trusts you with his records keeps you on. That's how it worked with our suppliers at the restaurant.

**Work and family** will carry us, not the government.
think: The thinking tasks are **Mr Blackwood's headache**, and I can help.

feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, like the restaurant's online orders.
S1.quote: My son Imran spent five years studying law, and now the first thing a computer learns is the junior lawyer's job.
fieldNote: She sees her **restaurant skills** as an asset in a changing farm.
Her one concern is **Imran's junior law** role.
She thinks being **trusted with records** protects her place.

steps.text: Set up an AI tracker for each hen house's laying rate and feed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for the thinking AI and 2031 for robots. I'd be sixty-three. Fast, but I'd want to be ready, not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock and families must stick together, the young ones especially will need help. I'd say government shouldn't smother it with rules, but it should stop a few giant companies owning everything. I'd say it at the mosque and to Imran's friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2031 a robot collects eggs and checks hens, and Fernley won't need me. That doesn't scare me much, we have the rent. What worries me is Imran, whose junior work goes in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd talk to Farid about buying a small egg unit of our own, two thousand hens, with robot collectors when they come. Imran could help run the business side if the law firm cuts him. I'd keep working at Fernley to learn everything I can before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy-minded, not scared. More worried for Imran than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the three years between 2028 and 2031 be for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprenticeship, really. I'd learn every part of Fernley so I could run our own unit. I'd use the three years before the robots to learn every corner of a hen house, so I'm the owner when they arrive and not the worker they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be risking savings at sixty. Isn't that a gamble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but we did it at thirty-six with the restaurant and it fed us for twenty-two years. With the building rent behind us, we can lose some and still eat. Farid will grumble and then agree.

say: Families must **stick together**, especially to help the young.
Government should stop **a few giant companies** owning everything without smothering it.
think: By **2031** a robot does my job at Fernley.
The rent covers us; I worry more about **Imran's junior work**.
do: Discuss buying a **two-thousand-hen unit** with Farid.
Bring Imran into **the business side** if he's cut.
Keep learning **every part** of Fernley before 2031.
S2.quote: I'd use the three years before the robots to learn every corner of a hen house, so I'm the owner when they arrive and not the worker they replace.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year gap** as an apprenticeship for ownership.
The **building rent** lets her take a risk at sixty.
Family worry centres on **Imran's career**, the household's thinking-work link.

steps.text: Look at buying a two-thousand-hen egg unit with Farid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031 and then robots in 2034. That gives me time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so families and small firms should get on with it. Learn the tools, start something, don't wait for the state. Same as I've always said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd work at Fernley till I want to stop. The egg unit idea could happen slower, with less risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving towards the egg unit and look at small plots for sale nearby. I'd test the AI flock tracker at Fernley first, to see what works before spending our money. And I'd keep the samosa stall going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Planning is my favourite part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nadia and Imran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's a pharmacist, she talks to patients, she'll adapt. Imran I'd tell to find the human side of law, the clients and the courtroom. My daughter Nadia hands out medicine with a kind word, and no machine has ever calmed a frightened old man the way Nadia does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk to you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The restaurant tenants, maybe, if people have less money to eat out. But Rahman's building is on the High Street, someone will always rent it. I'm not worried.

say: There's **time to prepare**, so families and small firms should get on with it.
**Start something** and don't wait for the state.
think: I'll work at Fernley **until I want** to stop.
The **egg unit** could happen slower and with less risk.
do: Save towards the **egg unit** and look at **nearby plots**.

S3.quote: My daughter Nadia hands out medicine with a kind word, and no machine has ever calmed a frightened old man the way Nadia does.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from a gamble into a **paced investment**.
She values **human contact** in her children's jobs.
Her only money risk is the **restaurant tenant**, which she dismisses.

steps.text: Save towards the egg unit and look at small plots nearby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for robots. I'd be seventy-one, and I'd hope to be teaching my grandchildren to cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and families should use it, not waste it complaining. Learn, save, start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's nothing frightening. I'd work at Fernley as long as my legs let me, then rest. The egg unit might become Imran's project, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Fernley and keep learning. Keep the samosa stall. Help Imran think about whether he wants to farm or stay in law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hopeful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years, my grandchildren grow up knowing it, and they won't be afraid. I started a restaurant at thirty-six and a farm job at fifty-six, so I'm not going to let a robot tell me I'm too old to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across the three fast pictures, what changes most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'm racing or strolling. With two years I'd be buying hens in a hurry at sixty, and with ten I'd hand the egg business plan to my son Imran.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, so families should use it, not complain.
**Learn, save, start something** is my advice to everyone.
think: It's **nothing frightening** for me; I'll work while my legs allow.
The egg unit might become **Imran's project**.
do: Keep the **samosa stall** at the farm shop.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be buying hens in a hurry at sixty, and with ten I'd hand the egg business plan to my son Imran.
fieldNote: Her **entrepreneurial streak** frames every scenario as a chance to start something.
Time decides **racing or strolling**, not whether she's safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, mostly for Imran, whose junior law work would go first, and because I'd have to rush the egg unit. What would help is small business loans for families starting farms with robots, and rules that stop a few giant firms owning all the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about older women. People think we're finished at sixty. I'd like someone to ask what we want to start, not just when we want to stop.

headlineQuote: I started a restaurant at thirty-six and a farm job at fifty-six, so I'm not going to let a robot tell me I'm too old to start something.
